message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold up to **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a month‑to‑month tenancy).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• Repairs that affect health or safety must be made promptly. | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) of needed repairs.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or seek a court order. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable (usually not more than 5% of the monthly rent). | • Keep receipts or bank records of payments.
• If you’re late, communicate with the landlord and negotiate a payment plan if needed. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month**: Either party may terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• **Fixed‑term**: The lease ends automatically unless renewed or extended.
• **Early termination**: Some leases allow early exit with a fee; otherwise, you may be liable for rent until a new tenant is found. | • Provide written notice (email or certified mail).
• Keep a copy of the notice and any acknowledgment from the landlord. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Report any harassment or disturbances to the landlord in writing. | | **Privacy** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24–48 hours) before entering the unit, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries and verify that the landlord followed notice requirements. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) if you suspect discrimination. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue, you may **deduct the cost** from your rent (up to the amount of the repair) and pay the landlord the remaining rent. | • Keep receipts and provide the landlord with a written notice of the deduction. | | **Eviction Process** | • The landlord must follow the Texas **eviction procedure**: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for nonpayment, 30‑day notice for lease violation), file a lawsuit, and obtain a court order. | • Respond to notices promptly.
• If you believe the eviction is unlawful, file a **motion to dismiss** or seek a **temporary restraining order** in court. | | **Legal Assistance** | • Texas offers free or low‑cost legal aid for tenants (e.g., Texas Legal Services Center, local bar association referral services). | • Contact a local tenant advocacy group or legal aid office for help. | #### Quick Tips 1. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of the lease, rent receipts, repair requests, and any correspondence with the landlord. 2. **Know the Timeline** – Texas law sets specific time frames for notice, repairs, and deposit returns; knowing these helps you assert your rights. 3. **Use Written Notices** – Even if you talk to the landlord, follow up with a written notice (email or certified mail) so you have proof. 4. **Seek Mediation First** – Many disputes can be resolved through mediation before going to court. The TDHCA offers mediation services for housing disputes. 5. **Know Your Local Ordinances** – Some cities in Texas have additional tenant protections (e.g., rent control, eviction moratoriums). Check your city’s housing department for local rules. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is general in nature and not legal advice. For specific legal questions or disputes, consult a licensed attorney or a local tenant advocacy organization.
